$comment: Idioms read off the page images of Carl Bratcher's ARP 2600 Patch Book to
Behringer 2600 conversion: 103 complete worked patches, each a full panel
diagram carrying a named musical intent, the routing drawn as coloured
cables, every slider marked, and the performer's notes underneath.
THERE IS NO TEXT IN THIS BOOK. It is a fixed-layout image EPUB, so a quote
anchor cannot reach it and OCR would capture the caption and throw away the
routing and the settings -- which is the entire content. These records are
anchored by page number AND the hash of that page image, because a page
number alone says only that the book is that long. See `_corpus_pages` in
provenance_check.py for why that is enough and a bare locator is not.
WHAT TRANSFERS, AND WHAT DOES NOT. The 2600 is a fixed semi-modular: three
oscillators, one filter, one sample-and-hold, a ring modulator, all half-
normalled to each other. A literal wiring list would be unbuildable in a
rack that has different modules, so what is encoded here is the TOPOLOGY
and the REASONING -- an oscillator running below hearing is the pattern
source, the sample-and-hold's rate is the tempo, a lag between the held
voltage and the pitch is what makes the steps glide. Where a patch leans on
something the 2600 has and a rack may not, the record says so.
AND WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT ENCODED. Several of these pages carry routing
that cannot be traced with confidence from a rendered image -- a coloured
line crossing a dense panel is a guess about which of four adjacent jacks it
lands on. Page 52's three-voice drum patch is one of those. Guessing would
produce a record that looks exactly like a read one and is fiction, which is
the failure this whole tier exists to prevent, so it is not here.

implies: make it sound like several players
idioms.is: Vibrato taken to each of several oscillators tuned in unison rather than to the pair as a whole, so the sound reads as several players who happen to agree rather than one instrument being wobbled.
idioms.sounds_right_when: it thickens into a section — you hear more than one player, and no single wobble you can follow.
idioms.source: ARP 2600 Patch Book to Behringer 2600 (Carl Bratcher), the Cello Section patch

anchor.shows: a panel diagram captioned Cello Section: two oscillators tuned in unison an octave below middle C, a third oscillator running below hearing taken to each of them for vibrato, and a note to add slight portamento

topology.describe: the modulator has to be split, because it has to reach more than one oscillator
a copy has to reach an oscillator's frequency input — one modulator on one oscillator of a pair is a detuned tone with a wobble in half of it
the oscillators have to be summed, or there is no ensemble to hear

listen_for.sounds_like: a small string section rather than a synthesizer: the players are together on the note and never quite together on the wobble, so the sound breathes without any one movement standing out
listen_for.confusable_with: a single oscillator with vibrato, which has one countable wobble, and a plain detuned pair, which beats at a fixed rate and does not breathe. The source's own instruction is to listen to each oscillator on its own and set its vibrato separately, which is the tell: the vibratos are meant to differ.

expect.why: an ensemble is still playing a note; if the pitch cannot be tracked for half the run the vibrato depth has gone past a section and into a chorus effect

common_mistakes.message: the vibrato never reaches an oscillator, so nothing wavers
the modulator is never split, so it can only reach one oscillator and the section is one player wide
the oscillators are never summed, so there is no section

implies: a pattern that slides between notes
idioms.is: A sample-and-hold clocked by an oscillator running below hearing, with the held voltage passed through a lag before it plays the note — so a repeating pattern arrives, and every interval in it is travelled rather than jumped.
idioms.sounds_right_when: a pattern recurs, and each move between its notes is audibly swooped rather than stepped.
idioms.source: ARP 2600 Patch Book to Behringer 2600 (Carl Bratcher), the Gliding Intervals patch

anchor.shows: a panel diagram captioned Gliding Intervals, with the third oscillator switched below hearing as the pattern source, the sample-and-hold in the signal path, the voltage processor's lag engaged, and notes to tune that oscillator for the pattern and the sample-and-hold's level for the size of the interval

topology.describe: something has to tell the sample-and-hold when to take a value — on the source instrument this is an oscillator switched below hearing, and its frequency is what sets the pattern
the held voltage has to pass through a lag, which is the whole difference between this and a stepped melody
the LAGGED voltage has to be what plays the note; patching the held voltage straight to pitch alongside it defeats the lag

listen_for.sounds_like: a line that never arrives cleanly: each note leans into the next, and because the sampled values repeat, the same swoops come round again. How far apart the notes are is one knob — the level of the sampled voltage — and how fast the pattern turns over is another.
listen_for.confusable_with: a stepped random melody, where every note lands square. If you cannot hear the journey between notes, nothing is lagging the voltage.

expect.why: fewer than three pitches is not a pattern, and the lag would have nothing to travel between

common_mistakes.message: nothing clocks the sample-and-hold, so it holds one value and the pattern never advances
the held voltage never reaches the lag, so the intervals step rather than glide
the lagged voltage never reaches a pitch input
